> **Proposed API, not runnable package documentation.** These examples follow
> `docs/api-vision.md` and have not been executed. All replies are scripted.
> The table helpers described here are part of the proposal.

A table is useful when each row keeps its identity and each column has a clear
meaning. Model work should follow the same rule: keep the input, the request,
the response, and any failed attempt distinct.

lm15 should make common analysis columns easy to obtain **without throwing
away the original objects**.

## Build a list column of requests

```r
library(lm15)

reviews <- tibble::tibble(
  id = c("a", "b", "c"),
  review = c("Easy to set up.", "Do not process this item.", "The screen is clear.")
)

requests <- purrr::map(reviews$review, function(review) {
  request(
    "demo-model",
    message_user(paste("Summarise this review:", review)),
    config = config(max_tokens = 80L)
  )
})
```

`tibble()` makes a data frame. `map()` applies a function to each input and
returns a list. Here each list element is one complete request value; nothing
has been sent.

Request and response values should have short structural summaries in list
columns, not enormous printed lists or snippets of sensitive content. Use
fields or serialization when you deliberately want to inspect the contents.

Tibble and purrr are optional companions. Core request construction and
execution do not require them.

## Capture one attempt per input

Set up three possible outcomes: an ordinary answer, a refusal, and a failed
request.

```r
client <- fake_lm(list(
  response("demo-model", message_assistant("Setup was easy."), "stop",
           usage = usage(input_tokens = 12L, output_tokens = 4L)),
  response("demo-model", message_assistant(refusal("I cannot process this item.")),
           "content_filter"),
  lm15_error("Try again later.", code = "rate_limit", retry_after = 2)
))

attempt <- purrr::safely(function(req) complete(client, req), quiet = TRUE)
attempts <- purrr::map(requests, attempt)
```

The application chose to capture failures and continue. `safely()` does not
retry; it returns separate `result` and `error` elements. This is ordinary
iteration in row order, not a provider batch job or an automatic retry engine.
On a real client, each attempt could incur a charge.

## Make an analysis view, not a new kind of response

```r
responses <- purrr::map(attempts, "result")
errors <- purrr::map(attempts, "error")

outcomes <- response_table(responses, errors = errors)
outcomes$id <- reviews$id
outcomes$request <- requests

outcomes[c("id", "has_response", "has_error", "text", "finish_reason", "error_code")]
```

The proposed `response_table()` is a pure, optional tibble adapter. It performs
no requests and makes no decisions about retries. It keeps one row per supplied
position, including missing results. The `.row` column is that one-based
position; your application supplies its own IDs.

The important columns have distinct meanings:

- `text` is a display/analysis view, with `NA` when the scalar text view is unavailable.
- `finish_reason` describes a received response; it is not an error code.
- `error_code` describes an LM15 failure, when there is one.
- `error_class` also preserves the identity of ordinary R failures without LM15 codes.
- `response`, `usage`, and `error` retain the complete objects in list columns.

Row `b` has a response but no ordinary text view because its content is a
refusal. Row `c` has an error and no response. A missing text value does not make
those rows equivalent.

```r
outcomes$response[[2]]$message$parts[[1]]$text
outcomes$error_class
retryable(outcomes$error[[3]])
```

`retryable()` classifies a failure. It neither retries nor promises a retry will
succeed. Inspect failures before choosing a recovery policy. A row with both
response and error is rejected by the table adapter rather than arbitrarily
choosing one. A row with neither is marked as having no supplied result, not
as a success.

## Request the column type you actually need

For just a text vector, you should not need to build a table:

```r
texts <- response_texts(responses)
```

This returns one character value per input, including `NA_character_` for
NULL entries and responses without an ordinary text view. The scalar
`response_text()` keeps its string-or-NULL contract; the plural helper is the
explicit analysis boundary. It does not rewrite refusal parts or tool calls.

For usage, choose between ordinary numeric analysis and exact decimal text:

```r
outcomes$input_tokens <- usage_dbl(responses, "input_tokens")
outcomes$input_tokens_exact <- usage_chr(responses, "input_tokens")
```

`usage_dbl()` always returns a double vector, using `NA_real_` for unreported
counts. It refuses values outside the exact double-integer range rather than
rounding them to make a column fit. `usage_chr()` always returns character and
preserves the exact decimal digits, including very large counts.

The default table leaves usage as a list column so it never silently makes
that choice for you. Counter field names are the exact canonical names, such
as `"input_tokens"`; partial spellings are not accepted.

```r
sum(outcomes$input_tokens)
```

If some counts are unknown, the total remains unknown. Dropping missing values
would produce only the sum of reported counts, not a complete bill. Keep that
qualification in the name or label of any partial total you publish.

## Save the representation you intend to keep

```r
outcomes$request_json <- purrr::map_chr(requests, as_json)
response_archive <- responses_json(responses, include_provider_data = FALSE)
```

`responses_json()` returns one JSON array string, preserving NULL positions.
Its provider-data policy is applied separately to each response. It does not
recursively clean the data inside those responses.

Choose `include_provider_data = TRUE` only when your application deliberately
needs the provider-owned payload too. That payload can be large or sensitive;
this is not a harmless pretty-printing option.

A saved request records what you asked for, not a promise that a model will
give the same answer tomorrow. Retain the actual response and appropriate run
metadata when you need to explain an analysis later.

## A small boundary, not a second analysis framework

The proposed helpers remove repeated extraction wrappers. They do not add
hidden row execution, flatten content parts into whatever columns happen to
exist, coerce every value to text, or fill absent usage with zero.

Use your usual R tools for grouping, filtering and joining. Use lm15 values to
retain the conversation and its meaning. For remote batches, see
[Files and jobs](jobs-and-resources.html).
